problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=xy\sqrt{{y}^{2}+1}$ along the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9.$

activity_context.topic_title: Line Integrals of Scalar Functions Over Circles

examples.knowledge_point: Computing a Line Integral of a Function Over a Circle
examples.problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y) =x^2-2$ along the circle $C$ with equation $x^2 + y^2 = 4.$
examples.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s  = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a circle of radius $2$ centered at $O.$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \big\langle 2\cos{t}, \: 2\sin{t} \big\rangle, \qquad 0 \le t \le 2\pi.
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{4({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y) = x^2-2,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}-2 \\  & =4{cos}^{2}⁡t-2 \\  & =2(2{cos}^{2}⁡t-1) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\cdot 2\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=2t,$ $\textrm d u=2\,\textrm d t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,\text{d}t & =2{\int }_{0}^{4\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡u{|}_{0}^{4\pi } \\  & =2(0-0) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14057418/assets/4403bd230338dee226429d3f8f3ac8eaede1152aff0b6b18bd2e7ad9f3a3b8e3.png)

Which of the following gives the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=9-{x}^{2}$ along a circle of radius $3,$ traversed from the point $(3,0)$ to the point $(0,3),$ as shown above?
feedback.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $3$ centered at $O.$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t+9{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{9({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=9-{x}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =9-(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =9-9{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =9{sin}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}9{sin}^{2}⁡t\cdot 3\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =27{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$
